Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space, let $x$ and $x'$ be
inertial charts whose transition is the affine map $x'(p)=\Lambda x(p)+b$ with
linear part $\Lambda$ (a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix by
[[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]), and let
$\Omega\subseteq A$ be an open subset. Let $J:\Omega\to V$, $k$ and $T$ be a
$\mathcal C^k$ vector field, a $\mathcal C^k$ covector field and a
$\mathcal C^k$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with components $J^a$, $k_a$ and
$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}$ in the chart $x$, and primed components in
the chart $x'$. Then:

(i) $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bJ^b$: a contravariant index gains the factor
$\Lambda^a{}_b$, that is, components transform by multiplication with the
transition matrix;

(ii) $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$: a covariant index gains the factor
$(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a$. If $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta_0$ is an affine scalar
function with constant covector $k$ and constant $\theta_0$, then
$\theta(p)=k'_ax'^a(p)+\theta'_0$ with $k'$ as above and
$\theta'_0:=\theta_0-k'_ab^a$, so the phase function is invariant when the
constant term is transformed together with the covector;

(iii) $T'^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}
=\Lambda^{a_1}{}_{c_1}\cdots\Lambda^{a_r}{}_{c_r}
(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}{}_{b_1}\cdots(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}{}_{b_s}
T^{c_1\dots c_r}{}_{d_1\dots d_s}$: every contravariant index gains a factor
$\Lambda$ and every covariant index a factor $\Lambda^{-1}$, and the law is
consistent with the multilinear evaluation of $T(p)$ after substituting the
transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant
index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy
$\eta'_{ab}=\eta_{ab}$;

(iv) the coordinate partial-derivative operators satisfy
$\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b$ when applied to scalar functions
at points where their coordinate representations are totally differentiable.
Consequently, at every event where the component functions of $J$ are totally
differentiable, the divergence is invariant,
$\partial'_aJ'^a=\partial_aJ^a$. These total differentials exist at every
event if $k\ge1$; for $k=0$ this clause applies only at events where the
specified components are totally differentiable, and does not assert
covariance from the existence of separate partial derivatives alone. For a
$\mathcal C^1$ type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ one has
$\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_c\partial_aT^{ac}$;

(v) alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each
slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies
$\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon_{abcd}$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$, whereas a general
Lorentz matrix with $\det=-1$ changes its sign;

(vi) let $J$ be a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field with components
$(J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3)$ in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as
$J_{\mathrm{cov}}:=(J^1,J^2,J^3)$ and denote by $\partial_i$ the spatial
partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation
$\partial_aJ^a=0$ is equivalent to
$\partial_0J^0+\sum_i\partial_iJ^i=0$, and under the passive boost with
parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$ ($\Lambda=B(\boldsymbol\beta)$,
$\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$) the components transform as
$J'^0=\gamma(J^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})$ and
$J'_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{cov}}
+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})\boldsymbol\beta
-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta J^0$;

(vii) if $U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ future timelike vector field and $\rho_0$ a
$\mathcal C^1$ scalar field, then $J:=\rho_0U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field
and its first component is $J^0=\rho_0U^0$. Future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$
in every inertial chart, so one may define the normalized chart direction
$u:=U/U^0$ and the coordinate density $\rho:=J^0$. Then $u^0=1$,
$u^i=U^i/U^0$, $\rho=\rho_0U^0$, and $J=\rho u$ pointwise. The coordinate
density $\rho$ and scalar multiplier $\rho_0$ are different objects:
$\rho=\rho_0$ if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-1)=0$; at points where
$\rho_0\neq0$ equality holds exactly when $U^0=1$. The vector $u$ is a
normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity
normalization. In an $x^0=ct$ convention the associated spatial coordinate
velocity, if interpreted as such, has components $cu^i$; physical
current/density identification requires its own model premise.

**Interpretation boundary.** The identification of a physical charge-current
with a vector field, and of $\rho$ with a measured charge density, is a model
premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the
transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert
that any physical current transforms as a vector.

Let $n$ be an observer congruence on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\nabla$ be the flat covariant derivative of the affine model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]), and write $n_b:=\eta_{bc}n^c$ for the associated covector field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

**(a) Rest metric and projection.** Define $h(v,w):=\eta(v,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)$ for vectors at the same point, so that $h=\eta+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ in components. Then $h(v,w)=\eta(h(v),h(w))$ for the orthogonal projection $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c). At every point $h$ is symmetric with radical spanned by $n(p)$, and its restriction to $n(p)^\perp$ is positive definite ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Acceleration.** The **acceleration** of the congruence is $a:=\nabla_nn$. Then $\eta(n,a)=0$ pointwise, because $2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)=n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=0$; consequently $a(p)$ is spacelike or zero by the causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is $c^2a$ and its magnitude is $c^2\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}$; the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

**(c) Kinematic decomposition.** Set $\theta_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}$ and $\omega_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}$, where $\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d+\nabla_dn_c)$ and $\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d-\nabla_dn_c)$. Then

$$\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab},$$

with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal ($\theta_{ab}n^b=\omega_{ab}n^b=n^a\theta_{ab}=n^a\omega_{ab}=0$), and this decomposition is unique with these properties. The tensor $\theta$ is the **expansion (and shear) tensor**, $\theta:=h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ is the **expansion scalar**, its trace-free part is the **shear**, and $\omega$ is the **vorticity 2-tensor**.

**(d) Born rigidity.** The congruence is **Born rigid** (it describes a rigid motion) when $\mathcal L_nh=0$. Since $(\mathcal L_nh)_{ab}=2\theta_{ab}$, Born rigidity is equivalent to $\theta=0$, equivalently to the projected symmetrized derivative of $n^\flat$ vanishing.

**(e) Scope.** These are kinematic definitions for a prescribed smooth field $n$ on the affine model; no dynamical equation, matter model, global synchronization or completeness is assumed, and $a$, $\theta$, $\omega$ and $h$ are local objects on $\Omega$.

Let $\pi:E\to M$ be a smooth vector bundle. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth, with smooth local extensions at any included endpoints. Give
$$\gamma^*E=\{(t,e)\in I\times E:\gamma(t)=\pi(e)\}$$
the subspace topology. For a bundle chart $\Phi:E|_U\to U\times\mathbb R^r$, writing $\Phi(e)=(\pi(e),v)$, the pulled-back chart and its inverse are
$$ (t,e)\longmapsto(t,v),\qquad (t,v)\longmapsto\bigl(t,\Phi^{-1}(\gamma(t),v)\bigr).$$
They are continuous for the subspace and product topologies, and the overlap maps are $(t,v)\mapsto(t,g_{\beta\alpha}(\gamma(t))v)$, hence smooth and fibrewise linear. Thus they directly define a smooth rank-$r$ bundle over $I$, with the stated smooth-up-to-endpoint convention. The interval $I$, as a subspace of $\mathbb R$, and the manifold $E$ are Hausdorff and second countable. Their product is Hausdorff by [[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]], and products of their two fixed countable bases form a countable basis. Hence both properties pass to the subspace $\gamma^*E$ by [[lem-t0-t1-and-hausdorff-are-hereditary]] and [[prop-second-countability-is-hereditary]].

A **section of $E$ along $\gamma$** is a smooth section of this bundle $\gamma^*E$. Equivalently it is a smooth map $V:I\to E$ with $\pi(V(t))=\gamma(t)$. For $E=TM$ it is a **vector field along $\gamma$**. In a pulled-back frame it has the form $V(t)=\sum_jv^j(t)e_j(\gamma(t))$ with arbitrary smooth coefficients $v^j$.

Values belong to the fibre over the parameter value, even if $\gamma(t)=\gamma(u)$ for $t\ne u$. For example, for a constant curve at $p$ and $v\ne0$ in $E_p$, the section $V(t)=tv$ is allowed and cannot be $s\circ\gamma$ for an ambient section $s$. Thus an ambient extension is not part of this definition.

For a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, use a finite subdivision into smooth pieces (each smooth up to its endpoints). A piecewise smooth section is continuous on the whole interval and smooth on each piece. On a singleton interval it is just a fibre vector; on an empty interval it is the empty section. These conventions define sections, without attempting differentiation on a singleton.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit
hyperboloid.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit
hyperboloid.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth vector fields on $M$. Their **Lie bracket** is the
operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

In a chart $(U,x^1,\dots,x^n)$, if

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, \qquad Y=\sum_{i=1}^n Y^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, $$

then on $U$

$$ [X,Y]=\sum_{j=1}^n \left(\sum_{i=1}^n X^i\partial_iY^j-Y^i\partial_iX^j\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}. $$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ consisting of the following four pieces of data.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are

  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of

Reading the dictionary [F1] in the primed chart, $E'_i=cF'^{0i}$ and $F'^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B'_k$, gives $E'_1=E_1$, $E'_2=\gamma(E_2-\beta cB_3)$, $E'_3=\gamma(E_3+\beta cB_2)$, $B'_1=B_1$, $B'_2=\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$ and $B'_3=\gamma(B_3-\beta E_2/c)$. Since $v=\beta ce_1$, the coordinate formulas of [F6] give $v\times B=\beta c\,(0,-B_3,B_2)$ and $v\times E=\beta c\,(0,-E_3,E_2)$; hence $(E+v\times B)_\perp=(0,E_2-\beta cB_3,E_3+\beta cB_2)$ and $(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp=(0,B_2+\beta E_3/c,B_3-\beta E_2/c)$, so the transverse formulas and the unchanged parallel components read $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$, $B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$, as claimed.

(Clause (c), rotation case; the orientation identity) Let $A\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ and $\det A=+1$, and let $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(1,A)$; then the components $F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$ of [F3] satisfy $E'=AE$ and $B'=AB$. First $F'^{0i}=A^i{}_jF^{0j}$, so $E'_i=cF'^{0i}=A^i{}_jE_j$. For the magnetic block, the dictionary gives $B'_q=\tfrac12\epsilon_{qij}F'^{ij}$, since inserting $F'^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijp}B'_p$ yields $\tfrac12\epsilon_{qij}\epsilon_{ijp}B'_p=\delta_{qp}B'_p$ by the elementary contraction $\epsilon_{qij}\epsilon_{ijp}=2\delta_{qp}$ (direct enumeration of the two contributing index pairs). Hence $B'_q=\tfrac12\epsilon_{qij}A^i{}_kA^j{}_l\epsilon_{klm}B_m$, and the matrix $A$ satisfies the cofactor identity $\epsilon_{qij}A^i{}_kA^j{}_l=A^q{}_m\epsilon_{mkl}$ for all $q,k,l$: the determinant of the matrix with columns $(c_m,c_k,c_l)$ of $A$ equals $\epsilon_{mkl}\det A=\epsilon_{mkl}$ by column alternation [F7], and it also equals $\sum_{n,i,j}\epsilon_{nij}A^n{}_mA^i{}_kA^j{}_l$ by the permutation expansion [F7]; multiplying that equality by $A^q{}_m$ and summing over $m$ turns the factor $A^q{}_mA^n{}_m$ into $(AA^{\mathsf T})^{qn}=\delta^{qn}$ and yields the identity, where $AA^{\mathsf T}=I_3$ holds because $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ with $\det A=1\ne0$ makes $A$ invertible with inverse $A^{\mathsf T}$ [F7]. Then $B'_q=\tfrac12A^q{}_m\epsilon_{mkl}\epsilon_{klp}B_p=A^q{}_m\delta_{mp}B_p=A^q{}_mB_m$ by the elementary identity $\epsilon_{mkl}\epsilon_{klp}=2\delta_{mp}$ (direct enumeration), so $B'=AB$. If $A$ is the matrix in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of a spatial rotation $R$ of the frame, then $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ and $\det A=+1$ by [F5], and $E'=RE$, $B'=RB$, which is the rotation case of clause (c).

(Conjugation of the vector boost) Let $v\in\mathbb R^3$ with $0<|v|<c$, put $u:=v/|v|$ and $\beta:=|v|/c\in(0,1)$, so $v/c=\beta u$. Among the standard basis vectors $e_1,e_2,e_3$ at most one is a multiple of $u$ (two independent vectors cannot both be nonzero multiples of one vector), so let $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ be the least index for which $e_j$ is not a multiple of $u$; set $\hat a:=\bigl(e_j-(e_j\cdot u)u\bigr)/\lVert e_j-(e_j\cdot u)u\rVert_2$, whose denominator is nonzero because $e_j$ is not a multiple of $u$, and $b:=u\times\hat a$. Then $(u,\hat a,b)$ is an orthonormal family, since $u\cdot\hat a=0$, $\lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert\hat a\rVert_2=1$, $b$ is orthogonal to $u$ and $\hat a$, and $\lVert b\rVert_2^2=\lVert u\rVert_2^2\lVert\hat a\rVert_2^2-(u\cdot\hat a)^2=1$ [F6]; it is positively oriented because $\det[u\ \hat a\ b]=\langle u\times\hat a,b\rangle=\lVert b\rVert_2^2=1$ [F6]. Let $S$ be the matrix with columns $u,\hat a,b$ and $R:=S^{\mathsf T}$, so the rows of $R$ are $u,\hat a,b$ and $Ru=e_1$; then $S^{\mathsf T}S=I_3$, $\det S=1$ and, since $\det S=1\ne0$, $S$ is invertible with $S^{-1}=S^{\mathsf T}$, so $SS^{\mathsf T}=I_3$, $R^{-1}=R^{\mathsf T}$ and $\det R=\det(S^{\mathsf T})=\det S=1$ [F7]. The conjugation identity $\widehat RB(v/c)\widehat R^{-1}=\Lambda_\beta$, where $\widehat R:=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$, follows by direct substitution in the matrix of [F2]: for all $x\in V$ set $y:=\widehat Rx$, so $y^0=x^0$, $y_{\mathrm{vec}}=Rx_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=R^{\mathsf T}y_{\mathrm{vec}}$; since $u\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}=u\cdot R^{\mathsf T}y_{\mathrm{vec}}=(Ru)\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $(v/c)\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}=\beta y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}$, the formula of [F2] with parameter $\beta u$ gives $(\widehat RB(v/c)x)^0=(B(v/c)x)^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta u\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})=\gamma(y^0-\beta y^1_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and $(\widehat RB(v/c)x)_{\mathrm{vec}}=R\bigl(R^{\mathsf T}y_{\mathrm{vec}}+(\gamma-1)y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}u-\gamma\beta y^0u\bigr)=y_{\mathrm{vec}}+(\gamma-1)y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}e_1-\gamma\beta y^0e_1$ using $(Ru)=e_1$; with $\widehat Rx=y$ this is exactly $\Lambda_\beta y$ by the matrix of [F2]. (Clause (a′): arbitrary-direction boost) Let $v\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|v|<c$. If $v=0$, then $B(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$ [F2], the charts differ by the translation $x'=x+b$, the components are unchanged by [F3], so $E'=E$ and $B'=B$, and the closed formulas reduce to the identity because $\gamma_v=1$ and all terms carrying $v$ vanish; no parallel direction is needed. Let $v\ne0$ and use $u,\hat a,b,S,R,\beta$ and the conjugation identity $B(v/c)=\widehat R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_\beta\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,S)\Lambda_\beta\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ of step 1.3. By [F3] the total component law of the composite is the matrix product of the factors of $B(v/c)=\widehat R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_\beta\widehat R$; applied successively, the first stage is the rotation $\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ (step 1.2 with $A=R$, whose hypotheses $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$ hold by step 1.3), giving $E''=RE$, $B''=RB$; the second stage is the axis boost $\Lambda_\beta$ in the intermediate frame, where step 1.1 applies because its proof uses only the dictionary and the component law; the third stage is the rotation $\widehat R^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{diag}(1,R^{\mathsf T})$ (step 1.2 with $A=R^{\mathsf T}$, whose hypotheses $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$ and $\det(R^{\mathsf T})=\det R=1$ hold by step 1.3 and [F7]), giving $E'=R^{\mathsf T}E'''$ and $B'=R^{\mathsf T}B'''$. Writing $\parallel,\perp$ for the components along $e_1$ in the intermediate coordinates, step 1.1 applied in the intermediate frame gives $E'''=E''_\parallel+\gamma(E''+\beta c\,e_1\times B'')_\perp$ and $B'''=B''_\parallel+\gamma(B''-\beta c\,e_1\times E''/c^2)_\perp$; applying $S=R^{\mathsf T}$ to the intermediate vectors and using the cross-product identity $R^{\mathsf T}(p\times q)=(R^{\mathsf T}p)\times(R^{\mathsf T}q)$ for the orthogonal matrix $R$ (obtained from the identity of step 1.2 by applying $R$ to both sides: $R\bigl((R^{\mathsf T}p)\times(R^{\mathsf T}q)\bigr)=(RR^{\mathsf T}p)\times(RR^{\mathsf T}q)=p\times q$) gives $R^{\mathsf T}(E''+\beta ce_1\times B'')=E+\beta c\,(R^{\mathsf T}e_1)\times(R^{\mathsf T}B'')=E+v\times B$, since $R^{\mathsf T}e_1=S e_1=u$ and $v=\beta cu$; moreover $R^{\mathsf T}E''_\parallel=(e_1\cdot E'')R^{\mathsf T}e_1=(u\cdot E)u=E_\parallel$ and $R^{\mathsf T}B''_\parallel=(u\cdot B)u=B_\parallel$. derivations.claim: (Clause (a): laboratory components of $e$ and $b$) By [F2], $n^0=\gamma_w$ and $n^i=\gamma_w w_i/c$, so with the dictionary [F1] the covariant components are $e_0=F_{00}n^0+F_{0i}n^i=-(\gamma_w/c^2)E\cdot w$ and $e_i=F_{i0}n^0+F_{ij}n^j=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}E_i+\frac{\gamma_w}{c}\epsilon_{ijk}w_jB_k=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}\bigl(E_i+(w\times B)_i\bigr)$, using $F_{i0}=-F_{0i}=E_i/c$ and $(w\times B)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}w_jB_k$ [F1]. For the dual, the definition $(*F)_{ab}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and the components of [F1] give $(*F)_{0i}=B_i$ and $(*F)_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}E_k/c$: indeed $\varepsilon_{0i}{}^{jk}=\varepsilon_{0ijk}=\epsilon_{ijk}$ because raising the two spatial indices is free and $(0,i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(0,1,2,3)$ exactly when $(i,j,k)$ is even, so $(*F)_{0i}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{jk\ell}B_\ell=B_i$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{jk\ell}=2\delta_{i\ell}$ (direct enumeration); and $\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}=\eta^{00}\eta^{kk}\varepsilon_{ij0k}=-\varepsilon_{ij0k}=-\epsilon_{ijk}$, since $(0,i,j,k)\mapsto(i,j,0,k)$ is an even permutation, so $(*F)_{ij}=\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}F_{0k}=(-\epsilon_{ijk})(-E_k/c)=\epsilon_{ijk}E_k/c$. Hence $b_0=(*F)_{00}n^0+(*F)_{0i}n^i=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}B\cdot w$ and $b_i=(*F)_{i0}n^0+(*F)_{ij}n^j=-\gamma_wB_i+\frac{\gamma_w}{c^2}\epsilon_{ijk}w_jE_k=-\gamma_w\bigl(B_i-\frac{(w\times E)_i}{c^2}\bigr)$. These are the four displayed component formulas of clause (a); in particular the laboratory temporal components $e_0,b_0$ need not vanish, so the orthogonality of the decomposition cannot be read as the vanishing of these laboratory components.

(Clause (a): annihilation, raising, reconstruction) Since $F$ and $*F$ are alternating, $e(n)=F_{ab}n^an^b=0$ and $b(n)=(*F)_{ab}n^an^b=0$; equivalently $n^ae_a=n^ab_a=0$ [F1]. For the metric-dual vectors $e^\sharp,b^\sharp$, defined by $\eta(e^\sharp,v)=e(v)$ and $\eta(b^\sharp,v)=b(v)$ for all $v$, this gives $\eta(e^\sharp,n)=\eta(b^\sharp,n)=0$, so $e^\sharp,b^\sharp\in n^\perp$; since both covectors annihilate $n$, restricting them to $n^\perp$ and raising with the positive rest metric of [F2] gives the same vectors, and this is the raising used in the definitions $E_n=c\,e^\sharp$, $B_n=-b^\sharp$. By [F1] the reconstruction $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ holds, and because the dictionary formulas of [F1] recover the six components of $F$ from $(e,b)$, the six rest components determine $F$ at the event. The measured vectors lie in the three-dimensional rest space $n^\perp$; they are not the laboratory coordinate triples $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$.

(Clause (a): the observer's inertial rest frame and the observed components) At $w=0$, $B(0)$ is the identity and $n=e_0$, so the rest frame is the laboratory frame and the displayed identity is immediate without a division by $|w/c|^2$. For $w\ne0$, applying the matrix of [F3] to the vector $n=\gamma_w(1,w/c)$ of [F2] gives $\bigl(B(w/c)n\bigr)^0=\gamma_w\bigl(\gamma_w-\frac{w}{c}\cdot\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}\bigr)=\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ and $\bigl(B(w/c)n\bigr)_{\mathrm{vec}}=\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}+\frac{\gamma_w-1}{|w/c|^2}\Bigl(\frac{w}{c}\cdot\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}\Bigr)\frac{w}{c}-\gamma_w\frac{w}{c}\gamma_w=\gamma_w\frac{w}{c}\bigl[1+(\gamma_w-1)-\gamma_w\bigr]=0$; hence $n$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$ in the chart $x'=B(w/c)x+b$, that is $n=e'_0$: the chart $x'$ is the observer's inertial rest frame, and it is an admissible inertial change of description because $B(w/c)$ is proper orthochronous [F3]. With $k(n)=k_an^a=-\frac{\omega}{c}\gamma_w+\frac{\omega}{c}\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\gamma_w=-\frac{\omega}{c}\gamma_w\bigl(1-\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\bigr)$ from [F2] and step 1.4, this gives $\omega_n=\gamma_w\bigl(1-\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\bigr)\omega>0$, where the positivity is clause (ii) of [F6], whose formula this is with the frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ of [F4] and the observer velocity $w$; its hypotheses hold by step 1.4 and the adopted model postulates [F5], [F6]. Each clause treats one model at a time, and step 1.5 uses one particle species, one rest mass and one rest parcel; the two factors of $\gamma^2\rho$ are matched one-to-one with particle energy and number density.
